macro: US equity futures are rallying Monday morning with S&P +49 points/65 basis points, Nasdaq +329 points/110 basis points, and the Russell 2000 +13.5 points/47 basis points, despite a weekend full of negative headlines. Asian and European markets are broadly higher, with the UN General Assembly kicking off this week as the primary driver of optimism around potential Middle East diplomatic progress. Brent crude is sliding 170 basis points to around $102.10, gold is down 60 basis points, and Treasuries have a bid with yields down 2-3 basis points across the curve.
rates_fed: Fed expectations are holding fairly steady with the market pricing in roughly 33 basis points of rate hikes over the final two meetings of the year, including roughly 50/50 odds of a hike at the October 28 meeting, and approximately 35 basis points of additional increases in 2027. The BOJ's recent rate hike was more dovish than anticipated, but monetary policy globally remains hawkish with the BOJ, ECB, and FOMC all hiking this month. Kansas City Fed President Schmid and Minneapolis Fed President Kashkari both made hawkish remarks, warning that elevated inflation is broad-based and not just an oil story. Treasury plans to issue over $1 trillion in T-bills over the next 12 months, pushing bill supply above 24% of marketable debt and above the Treasury's own 20% target.
market_outlook: Adam's lean is cautiously mixed — the equity strength feels confounding given uniformly negative weekend news flow, and the rally is almost entirely driven by diplomatic optimism around the UN General Assembly. The key catalyst to watch is whether any tangible progress on Middle East tensions or Iran diplomacy emerges this week, as even a modest improvement in the geopolitical picture could trigger a meaningful drop in oil prices with powerful favorable knock-on effects across the entire macro landscape.
bull_case: Nearly all of the market's macro headaches trace back to oil, meaning even a small diplomatic breakthrough at the UN General Assembly this week could trigger an outsized drop in energy prices. Lower oil would cascade into lower yields, eased inflation pressure, margin relief, and improved consumer confidence. China and Pakistan are reportedly urging Iran to rein in the Houthis, signaling growing global alarm and potential pressure toward de-escalation. The Trump-Xi summit on September 24 could also yield modest tariff reductions, adding another incremental positive.
bear_case: The weekend news flow was nearly uniformly negative — Houthis dramatically escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia, Ukraine launched its largest drone strike on Russia, and a deluge of troubling AI headlines hit after Friday's close including a delayed Anthropic IPO, weak Anthropic 2027 ARR projections, massive OpenAI cash burn, and Oracle data center debt problems. Inflation remains hot and broad-based with multiple central banks in hiking mode, and US-China trade truce extension talks have stalled. Any optimism around the UN General Assembly could easily prove to be wishful thinking, and the geopolitical landscape is deteriorating on multiple fronts simultaneously.

company_items.summary: Disney's parks business is outperforming peers, many of whom are seeing traffic headwinds, thanks to price promotions and package deals. The company appears to be gaining market share in the theme park segment through targeted discounting strategies. This is a positive data point for Disney at a time when consumer spending on travel and experiences is under scrutiny.

Novo Nordisk shares are slumping in European trading after the company failed to provide more granular financial targets at its Monday analyst meeting, disappointing investors who were looking for greater specificity on the path to future blockbuster launches. The lack of concrete guidance is being interpreted as a negative signal. Shares are underperforming in Europe on Monday.

Oracle was the subject of a negative Financial Times article over the weekend focusing on poor price action in debt tied to a massive Oracle-linked data center in New Mexico known as Project Jupiter. Efforts to offload loans tied to the facility have reportedly hit a wall, raising concerns about off-balance sheet data center liability exposure. This adds to the broader negative AI infrastructure sentiment from the weekend.

Paramount is in advanced settlement talks with California to resolve a lawsuit against its Warner Bros. Discovery merger deal. As part of the settlement, Paramount could agree to preserve CNN's editorial independence and divest certain cable channels including Comedy Central, though not all state attorneys general involved are on board. The outcome remains uncertain and the path to deal closure still faces regulatory friction.

Potential concessions include preserving CNN's editorial independence and divesting cable assets like Comedy Central. Not all state AGs are aligned, keeping deal risk elevated.

Kuehne and Nagel, the European logistics giant, announced a long-term strategic collaboration with Amazon and its shares are outperforming in Europe as a result. The deal suggests Amazon continues to build out and deepen its logistics and supply chain partnerships globally. The announcement is incrementally positive for Amazon's logistics network strategy.

London-based neocloud firm Nscale filed its S1 publicly on Friday afternoon and aims to list on the NYSE under the ticker NSCL. The company is entering a crowded AI infrastructure market at a time when investor sentiment toward the sector is under pressure from OpenAI cash burn concerns and Anthropic IPO delays. The timing of the public filing is notable given the difficult AI funding backdrop.

Costco is scheduled to report earnings Thursday night this week, making it one of the marquee earnings events of the week. The print will be closely watched for any read on consumer health given the macro pressure from elevated energy prices and persistent inflation. No pre-announcement or guidance update has been issued.

tts_summary:
Good morning. Let's get into it.

Markets are kicking off the week with a rally that frankly doesn't match the weekend news flow. S&P futures are up about 49 points or 65 basis points, Nasdaq is up 110 basis points, and the Russell 2000 is up 47 basis points. Europe is up 85 to 120 basis points, Asia closed broadly higher with Korea up 165 basis points and Hong Kong up over 1 percent. Treasuries have a bid, yields are down 2 to 3 basis points across the curve, and Brent crude is sliding 170 basis points to around 102 dollars and 10 cents.

Here's the thing — nearly every headline from the weekend was net negative. Houthis dramatically escalated their missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia. Ukraine launched its largest drone strike on Russia of the entire war. And after Friday's close, a wave of troubling AI headlines hit: Anthropic's IPO is delayed, their 2027 revenue projections disappointed, OpenAI is projecting roughly 280 billion dollars in negative free cash flow through 2030, and Oracle's Project Jupiter data center debt has reportedly hit a wall with lenders. That is a lot of bad news to look past.

So what's driving the green? One word: diplomacy. The UN General Assembly runs from September 22nd through the 28th in New York, and Trump has signaled he'd be open to meeting with Iran's president, who is expected to attend. Trump also reportedly called off air strikes against the Houthis at the last minute Sunday night. The bull thesis here is simple — almost every macro problem right now traces back to oil. If geopolitical progress, even modest progress, causes energy prices to sustainably drop, you get lower yields, less hawkish monetary policy, margin relief, and better consumer confidence all at once. That's the cascade markets are hoping for.

The bear case is equally straightforward. The geopolitical situation is genuinely bad and getting worse on multiple fronts. Inflation is hot and broad-based — both Kansas City Fed President Schmid and Minneapolis Fed President Kashkari made hawkish comments over the weekend warning that inflation is spreading beyond energy into every corner of the economy. The Fed is pricing in another roughly 33 basis points of hikes by year-end with roughly even odds of a move at the October 28th meeting. Treasury is also planning to flood the market with over a trillion dollars in T-bills over the next 12 months, pushing short-term supply well above its own target. The UN General Assembly optimism could very easily prove to be wishful thinking.

On the company side, Novo Nordisk is sliding in Europe after disappointing investors at its analyst meeting with a lack of specific financial targets. Oracle remains in focus after that negative data center debt story. Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery are in advanced settlement talks with California over their merger, with potential concessions including divesting cable channels — deal risk remains elevated. On the positive side, Disney's parks business is outperforming peers using price promotions, and Amazon scored a long-term logistics partnership with Kuehne and Nagel.

The big catalysts to watch this week are the Trump-Xi summit on Thursday, the flash September PMIs Wednesday morning, and whatever comes out of the UN General Assembly on the Middle East diplomacy front. Costco reports Thursday night.

Bottom line — the rally feels fragile and event-driven. The geopolitical and monetary policy backdrops are both still working against you. Stay disciplined.
